title: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset
hook: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset — why sunset is the clock

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabbat. To stop, from Friday sunset to Saturday stars. Your line was stop. it's already Friday. Did you find ten minutes with nothing to finish? Day four.

It's Friday afternoon in a Jewish home, and the clock is running. The oven is on. Someone is still in the shower. A kid can't find their shoes. Then, at a set minute, printed on a calendar on the fridge, it all has to be done. Someone stands at the table, strikes a match, and lights two candles. They circle their hands over the flames three times, cover their eyes, and whisper a blessing. When they uncover their eyes, the week is over. Eighteen minutes before sunset, in many towns. Today: two small flames, and why the sun keeps the clock.
screen: `FRIDAY. THE CLOCK IS RUNNING.` → `A MATCH, TWO FLAMES.` → `HANDS OVER THE EYES.`

segments.voice: Start with the clock. Yesterday you heard that a Jewish day starts in the evening. Here's the line behind it. In the first chapter of the Torah, every day of creation closes the same way. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Evening first, so Shabbat arrives with the dark on Friday. And since lighting a fire is one of the thirty-nine kinds of work that stop, the flames have to be lit while it's still day. Many communities light eighteen minutes early, a margin, so nobody is caught lighting late. Jerusalem traditionally lights forty minutes before. Why two? Because the Sabbath commandment appears twice in the Torah, in two wordings. In Exodus: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy: "Observe the sabbath day, to keep it holy." Remember and observe. Zachor and shamor. One flame for each. Many families add a candle for every child, so the table gets brighter as the family grows. Then the eyes. Usually you say a blessing and then do the thing. But once the blessing is said, Shabbat has begun and lighting is no longer allowed. So people light first, cover their eyes, say the blessing, and then open them, as if seeing the light for the first time. And why candles at all? The Talmud asks: if you're poor, and can only afford one light, and it's both Shabbat and Hanukkah, which do you buy? The Shabbat light, it says, for the sake of peace in the home. Shalom bayit. Not a light to read by. A light so the family can see each other's faces at dinner.
screen: `EVENING FIRST, THEN MORNING.` · `REMEMBER, AND OBSERVE.` · `LIGHT, THEN BLESS, THEN SEE.` · `A LIGHT FOR PEACE IN THE HOME.` · then, large: `TWO FLAMES.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. If there's a light near you, a lamp or a candle or even your screen, look at it. First breath: remember something good from this week. Second breath: let it be enough. Third breath: close your eyes, the way people do after lighting, and then open them slowly, as if the light is new.
The candles. Two flames lit before sunset on Friday, remember and observe, for peace in the home. Fourth word.
Your line: light, then rest. Tonight, before you stop for the day, turn on one light on purpose, a lamp or a candle, and let it mean the work is done. Day four.

howItsDone: In many Jewish homes a woman of the house, or anyone present, lights at least two candles before sunset on Friday, circles her hands over them, covers her eyes and says the blessing, and Shabbat begins.
